newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to renew drive to ban tobacco adverts.
newsitem.headline: EU to renew drive to ban tobacco adverts.

text.p: The European Commission said Tuesday it would renew attempts to introduce a European Union-wide ban on tobacco advertising, following the new British government's announcement on Monday of a national ban.

Last November, EU health ministers shelved efforts to prohibit tobacco advertising in the face of resistance from some member countries, adopting instead a resolution urging governments to continue coordinated anti-smoking efforts.
Britain's former Conservative government sided for many years with the Netherlands, Germany, Greece and Denmark in blocking adoption of an EU-wide ban.

But if the new British Health Secretary Frank Dobson follows up on the national ban announced on Monday with efforts to change minds in Europe, it would be possible to outlaw tobacco advertising throughout the 15-member bloc.
At the moment, 10 EU countries have some form of restrictions on cigarette marketing but the commission has argued that the effectiveness of these bans is limited.

A spokeswoman for European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said the commission, the EU executive body, was delighted with London's new policy and would revive a possible EU-wide ban when health ministers meet in Luxembourg in June.
But she said she did not expect a more concrete decision until later this year, when Luxembourg takes over the presidency of the EU.
Britain's new Labour government announced on Monday a ban on advertising, which had been expected, but added that it was also banning cigarette makers from sponsoring sports events.

Anti-smoking campaigners welcomed the move but tobacco companies said they were disappointed by a decision. Cigarette companies spend millions sponsoring sports such as cricket, golf, darts, rugby, show-jumping and Formula One motor racing.
A U.S. judge in North Carolina ruled in April that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration could regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes, but had no authority over advertising.
But a growing number of cities in the United States have moved to ban cigarette advertising near places where children gather.
